questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has 7 months of cough, wheeze and chest tightness. She had no chest problems as a child. Eight months ago she started work as a technician in a laboratory that breeds mice and rats. Her symptoms are worst in the evenings after work and clear during a two week holiday abroad. Her chest is clear today.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New asthma symptoms starting after a new job (laboratory animal allergens) and improving away from work is occupational asthma; she had no previous asthma to exacerbate.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: no chest problems as a child
clear during a two week holiday
steps.x: New adult-onset wheeze after a new job, better away from work.

elim: No smoking history, and it does not improve on holiday.
Can cause cough but not wheeze that clears away from work.
Gives fever, myalgia and crackles hours after exposure, not wheeze.
She had no asthma before this job.

steps.x: D: Occupational asthma. Late-onset asthma after a new job that improves on holiday = occupational asthma.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has worked for a year in a car body repair shop, spraying two-pack polyurethane paint. Over the last 6 months he has developed wheeze, cough and breathlessness that are worse at work and improve at weekends. He does not smoke. His peak flow falls during work shifts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative agent?
questions.e: Isocyanates in two-pack spray paints are the commonest cause of occupational asthma; asbestos, coal and silica cause pneumoconioses.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely causative agent?

clues: peak flow falls during work shifts
steps.x: Spray painting + occupational asthma picture.

elim: Causes pleural plaques, asbestosis and mesothelioma, not asthma.
Causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis.
A cause of baker's asthma, but he is a spray painter.
Causes silicosis in quarry workers and sandblasters.

steps.x: D: Isocyanates. Isocyanates (spray painting, foam, adhesives) are the commonest cause of occupational asthma.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has had wheeze and cough for 9 months. She has no history of childhood asthma and does not smoke. She works in a factory making polyurethane foam. Her GP suspects she has occupational asthma rather than ordinary adult-onset asthma.
questions.q: Which feature of her history would most strongly support an occupational cause?
o: A family history of hay fever
Symptoms improve when she is on holiday
questions.e: Improvement away from work (holidays, weekends) is the key history in occupational asthma; the other triggers occur in any asthma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of her history would most strongly support an occupational cause?

clues: occupational asthma rather than ordinary adult-onset asthma
steps.x: What separates occupational from non-occupational asthma?

elim: Atopy raises the risk of any asthma; it does not point to work.
Common to all asthma.
A common trigger of ordinary asthma.
Cold air triggers any asthma.

steps.x: D: Symptoms improve when she is on holiday. Classic: late-onset asthma after a new job that improves on holiday/away from work.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has 3 years of worsening breathlessness. He fitted asbestos insulation in ships for 20 years. He has clubbing and fine bibasal crackles. HRCT shows bilateral lower lobe fibrosis and calcified pleural plaques. He has spirometry.
questions.q: Which is the most likely spirometry result?
questions.e: Asbestosis gives a restrictive pattern: FEV1 and FVC both below 80% with a preserved ratio of 0.7 or more.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely spirometry result?
Asbestosis = fibrosis = restriction.

elim: A low ratio is obstructive, as in COPD.
Obstructive pattern with normal FVC.
Normal; his fibrosis would reduce volumes.
Normal values do not fit established asbestosis.

steps.x: C: FEV1 68% predicted, FVC 64% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.82. Asbestosis: restrictive spirometry (FEV1 and FVC below 80%, FEV1/FVC at least 0.7).

questions.stem: A 69 year old retired builder has a chest X-ray before a hernia operation. He has no breathing symptoms and his chest is clear. He removed old asbestos roofing and ceiling tiles for many years. The X-ray shows bilateral discrete calcified opacities on the diaphragmatic and lateral pleura. The lung fields are clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Calcified pleural plaques are a marker of past asbestos exposure and are benign; asbestosis needs parenchymal fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: discrete calcified opacities on the diaphragmatic and lateral pleura
steps.x: Asymptomatic asbestos-exposed builder with calcified pleural patches only.

elim: Needs lung fibrosis with crackles and restriction; his lungs are clear.
Gives pain, weight loss and effusion or pleural thickening, not asymptomatic calcified plaques.
Shows hilar nodes, not pleural calcification.
Upper zone nodules and eggshell hilar calcification.

steps.x: C: Pleural plaques. Pleural plaques on CXR mark asbestos exposure in construction workers.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man worked as a shipyard boilermaker for 25 years. He has 3 months of dull left-sided chest pain, breathlessness and weight loss. There is dullness and reduced breath sounds at the left base. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources). A pleural aspirate is sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pleural fluid result?
o: Empyema with pH 6.9 and frank pus
Exudate with protein 44 g/L and high LDH
Transudate with protein 18 g/L and low LDH
Transudate with protein 22 g/L in a heart failure pattern
questions.e: Malignant mesothelioma effusions are exudates (protein above 35 g/L, LDH above two thirds of the upper limit of normal); transudates point to cardiac, liver or renal failure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely pleural fluid result?
Asbestos exposure + chest pain + weight loss + effusion = mesothelioma.

elim: Follows thoracic duct injury or lymphoma.
Infection with fever, not a slow painful malignant effusion.
Seen in heart, liver or kidney failure, not malignancy.
He has no heart failure; a malignant effusion is exudative.

steps.x: C: Exudate with protein 44 g/L and high LDH. Mesothelioma effusion is exudative: LDH above 2/3 of the upper reference limit, protein above 35 g/L.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has worked for 30 years as a sandblaster. He has silicosis with upper zone nodular fibrosis on chest X-ray. He is HIV negative and does not have diabetes. He asks what other problems his lung disease may lead to.
questions.q: Which complication is he at greatest increased risk of?
questions.e: Silica is toxic to alveolar macrophages, so silicosis greatly increases the risk of tuberculosis; mesothelioma is an asbestos disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which complication is he at greatest increased risk of?
Silica damages alveolar macrophages.

elim: Not a characteristic complication of silicosis.
Linked to asbestos, not silica.
Needs immunosuppression such as HIV, which he does not have.
Not specifically linked to silica.

steps.x: E: Pulmonary tuberculosis. Silicosis increases the risk of TB.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has slowly worsening breathlessness over 10 years and coughs up black sputum. He worked for 30 years in a job underground in South Wales. He never smoked. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources). It shows small rounded opacities and larger conglomerate masses in both upper zones.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Upper zone nodular fibrosis with conglomerate masses.

questions.q: Which is the most likely occupational cause?
questions.e: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis follows coal dust exposure; upper zone nodules coalescing into masses is progressive massive fibrosis. Mining is a classic at-risk job.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely occupational cause?

clues: larger conglomerate masses in both upper zones
steps.x: Black sputum, underground work, upper zone nodules and masses.

elim: Causes occupational asthma from isocyanates.
Causes farmer's lung (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).
Asbestos exposure, giving basal fibrosis and plaques.
Flour causes occupational asthma.

steps.x: B: Coal mining. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis: coal dust exposure causing progressive lung disease.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man works in a malting house turning damp germinating barley. He has 6 months of breathlessness and dry cough, with episodes of fever and aching muscles starting several hours after a shift. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are fine crackles at both mid zones.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent fever, myalgia, cough and breathlessness hours after mouldy organic dust exposure is hypersensitivity pneumonitis (malt worker's lung); asthma gives wheeze without fever.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fever and aching muscles starting several hours after a shift
steps.x: Organic dust, delayed fever and myalgia, crackles.

elim: Needs asbestos exposure and causes slow basal fibrosis without fevers.
Would not recur with each shift.
Gives wheeze without fever, myalgia or crackles.
Mineral dust, not organic mould; no fevers.

steps.x: C: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: organic dust exposure, immune-mediated cough and breathlessness.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has 18 months of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. For 8 years he has cut and polished engineered quartz kitchen worktops, often dry-cutting without a mask. He never smoked. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. HRCT shows multiple small nodules in both upper lobes with enlarged calcified hilar nodes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Engineered quartz is almost pure silica; heavy exposure causes accelerated silicosis with upper lobe nodules and calcified hilar nodes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: small nodules in both upper lobes
steps.x: Heavy crystalline silica exposure and upper lobe nodules.

elim: Lower lobe fibrosis after asbestos, with pleural plaques.
Needs coal dust exposure.
Organic antigen with fevers, not mineral dust.
Can cause upper zone nodules and hilar nodes, but his heavy silica exposure explains it.

steps.x: E: Silicosis. Silicosis: silica exposure (mining, sandblasting, stone cutting) causing upper lobe fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has developed wheeze and chest tightness since he started working in a foam moulding factory. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. He has scattered expiratory wheeze. Spirometry is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely spirometry finding?
o: Normal spirometry with a raised TLCO
Obstructive pattern with significant reversibility after salbutamol
questions.e: Occupational asthma gives reversible airflow obstruction; restriction with low TLCO fits fibrotic diseases like asbestosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely spirometry finding?
Occupational asthma = asthma: reversible obstruction.

elim: Suggests COPD, not asthma.
Wheeze on examination makes obstruction likely; raised TLCO is not typical.
Suggests chest wall or muscle disease.
Seen in fibrotic conditions such as asbestosis.

steps.x: C: Obstructive pattern with significant reversibility after salbutamol. Spirometry: obstructive in occupational asthma, restrictive in fibrotic conditions.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman worked for 25 years in a factory spinning asbestos into textile yarn. She has had slowly progressive breathlessness for 4 years. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. She has clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. She has never smoked.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Heavy asbestos exposure with progressive breathlessness, clubbing and basal crackles is asbestosis, a chronic progressive fibrotic disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
steps.x: Heavy asbestos exposure + basal fibrosis signs.

elim: Never smoker, and COPD does not cause clubbing.
Needs coal dust exposure and is upper zone.
Needs organic antigen exposure.
Gives wheeze, not clubbing and basal crackles.

steps.x: A: Asbestosis. Respiratory symptoms + relevant job exposure = suspect occupational lung disease.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman works on a car seat production line using isocyanate foam. She records her peak flow four times a day for 4 weeks, including work days and rest days. Her GP wants to know which pattern would best support occupational asthma (see item resources).

visual.title: Mean daily peak flow
visual.caption: Falls through the working week, recovers at the weekend.

questions.q: Which peak flow pattern would most support the diagnosis?
o: Higher readings on work days than on rest days
Low readings only in the first hour after waking
Lower readings on work days, recovering on rest days
Steady fall over 4 weeks regardless of work
questions.e: A serial peak flow diary showing falls on work days with recovery on rest days supports occupational asthma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which peak flow pattern would most support the diagnosis?
Look for a work-related pattern.

elim: The opposite of the expected pattern.
Does not suggest asthma at all.
Morning dipping occurs in any asthma.
Not linked to work exposure.

steps.x: D: Lower readings on work days, recovering on rest days. Serial peak flow in and out of work diagnoses occupational asthma.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has just been diagnosed with silicosis after 30 years in a granite quarry. He has no fever, weight loss or night sweats and his sputum is scant. He is about to be reviewed in clinic and his routine bloods are normal.
questions.q: Which additional investigation should routinely be done?
questions.e: Silicosis increases TB risk, so TB testing (e.g. IGRA) is part of the work-up even without symptoms.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional investigation should routinely be done?

clues: no fever, weight loss or night sweats
steps.x: Silicosis raises TB risk: screen.

elim: Not needed; history and imaging make the diagnosis.
A marker for sarcoidosis.
For hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
For cystic fibrosis.

steps.x: B: Interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Investigations include routine bloods and TB testing.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is referred with 2 years of progressive breathlessness and fine crackles at both bases. HRCT shows basal fibrosis. His GP letter says he 'worked in the building trade' but gives no further detail. He has never smoked and takes no medicines.
questions.q: Which is the most important next step in assessing the cause?
questions.e: A detailed occupational history (jobs, materials, asbestos, protection, dates) with imaging is central to diagnosing occupational lung disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important next step in assessing the cause?
Construction work + fibrosis: what exactly did he do?

elim: Invasive; the history may make the diagnosis.
Delays diagnosis and adds little.
For sarcoidosis, which is upper zone.
No infection is suggested.

steps.x: E: Take a detailed occupational history. A detailed occupational history plus imaging is the key to diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 66 year old retired electrician has mild exertional breathlessness. He drilled through asbestos boards for years. His chest X-ray is normal, but his spirometry shows FVC 78% predicted with FEV1/FVC 0.80 and there are faint basal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging to look for early disease?
o: Repeat chest X-ray in a year
questions.e: CT is more sensitive than chest X-ray for early fibrosis and pleural plaques, so it is used when the X-ray is normal but disease is suspected.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate imaging to look for early disease?
Suspected early asbestosis with a normal X-ray.

elim: Useful for effusions, not lung fibrosis.
Assesses diaphragm palsy, not fibrosis.
Less sensitive and delays diagnosis.
Looks for pulmonary emboli.

steps.x: B: CT chest. CT chest is more sensitive than CXR for fibrosis, nodules and pleural plaques.

questions.stem: A 35 year old baker sees his GP with 5 months of wheeze and cough that are worse at work. He has no previous asthma. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest is clear today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Spirometry with reversibility shows the obstructive pattern of asthma first; serial peak flows then link it to work.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: wheeze and cough that are worse at work
steps.x: Suspected occupational asthma: first show obstruction.

elim: Usually normal in asthma and does not show airflow obstruction.
Looks for fibrosis, not asthma.
For hypersensitivity pneumonitis, not asthma.
No role.

steps.x: E: Spirometry with reversibility testing. First-line: spirometry (obstructive in occupational asthma); then serial peak flows in and out of work.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a new right pleural effusion. He worked as a plumber lagging pipes in the 1970s. He has right chest wall pain and has lost 5 kg. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A unilateral effusion in an asbestos-exposed man with pain and weight loss needs ultrasound-guided aspiration for protein, LDH and cytology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Unilateral effusion with asbestos exposure and weight loss.

elim: Does not sample pleural fluid.
For occupational asthma.
For sarcoidosis.
Will not explain a unilateral effusion.

steps.x: E: Ultrasound-guided diagnostic pleural aspiration. Sample the fluid: mesothelioma gives an exudate (protein above 35 g/L, high LDH).

questions.stem: A 53 year old dairy farmer has hypersensitivity pneumonitis confirmed by positive serum precipitins. He has recurrent attacks after forking mouldy hay in winter. Between attacks he is well. His oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air today. He wants to keep farming.
questions.q: Which is the most important step in management?
o: Long-term oral prednisolone while continuing exposure
questions.e: Avoiding the antigen (drying hay, changing practices, a respirator) is central in hypersensitivity pneumonitis; steroids do not replace it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important step in management?
Identified antigen; attacks with exposure.

elim: HP is not an IgE-mediated allergy.
Steroids do not replace removing the antigen.
He is not hypoxic.
Does not treat the cause of HP.

steps.x: A: Avoid exposure to mouldy hay. Remove the trigger: avoiding the causative agent is central.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man sees his GP with 2 years of worsening breathlessness. He worked in a shipyard for 30 years. He has fine bibasal crackles. Chest X-ray shows basal reticular shadowing and pleural plaques. He has had no tests at the hospital.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Refer to a respiratory specialist to confirm the diagnosis
Repeat chest X-ray in a year
questions.e: Suspected asbestosis should be referred to secondary care to confirm the diagnosis (CT, lung function), which also matters for compensation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Suspected occupational lung disease in primary care.

elim: Does not treat fibrosis.
Delays diagnosis and support.
No infection is present.
Steroids are not used in asbestosis.

steps.x: B: Refer to a respiratory specialist to confirm the diagnosis. First: confirm the diagnosis and refer to secondary care.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has hypersensitivity pneumonitis from mould in his workplace. He moved to a new site a month ago. He remains breathless with crackles, oxygen saturation 90% breathing air and widespread ground-glass change on HRCT. Infection has been excluded.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: If HP stays active despite removing the antigen, oral corticosteroids are used to settle the inflammation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?

clues: moved to a new site a month ago
steps.x: Exposure removed but still significant disease.

elim: Will not settle alveolar inflammation.
Infection has been excluded.
An antifibrotic for IPF and progressive fibrosis, not active inflammation.
For asthma, not hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

steps.x: E: Oral prednisolone. Long-term: bronchodilators for asthma; steroids in some cases.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has simple silicosis from 25 years as a quarry worker. He has stopped working with silica. He is mildly breathless on hills. His oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. TB testing is negative. He asks how his condition will be followed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?
questions.e: Occupational lung diseases are chronic and can progress, so lung function is monitored over time; steroids and oxygen are not needed now.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?

clues: how his condition will be followed
steps.x: Chronic, potentially progressive disease.

elim: Invasive and unnecessary.
Silicosis can progress even after exposure stops.
Steroids do not alter silicosis.
He is not hypoxic.

steps.x: E: Regular lung function monitoring. Monitor lung function over time.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man comes to the emergency department with 3 months of increasing breathlessness. He works as a sandblaster at a shipyard. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows upper zone nodules. The admitting doctor does not record his job.
questions.q: Which is the most important omission in his assessment?
questions.e: In breathlessness with possible occupational exposure (sandblasting: silica), the occupational history is critical to assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important omission in his assessment?
Breathlessness + relevant exposure: ask about work.

elim: Not relevant to his nodular lung disease.
Upper zone nodules point to dust exposure, not asthma.
Less relevant than his job given the X-ray.
Does not explain upper zone nodules.

steps.x: D: An occupational exposure history. Breathlessness with a relevant occupational exposure: assess for occupational lung disease.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has occupational asthma from latex gloves, confirmed in a specialist clinic. She is a theatre nurse. She uses salbutamol several times a day at work and is well on holidays. Her employer can provide latex-free gloves for the whole theatre team.
questions.q: Which is the most important step in management?
o: Change to a latex-free work environment
questions.e: Avoiding the sensitiser (a latex-free environment) is the key treatment in occupational asthma; drugs alone allow ongoing sensitisation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important step in management?
Identified trigger that can be removed.

elim: Not standard; removing exposure is the key step.
Masks symptoms while exposure continues.
Not a substitute for removing the trigger.
LABA without ICS is unsafe in asthma and does not remove the cause.

steps.x: A: Change to a latex-free work environment. Removing the trigger is central; bronchodilators for symptoms.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has advanced coal workers' pneumoconiosis. He is breathless at rest. His resting oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air on two occasions 4 weeks apart. Arterial blood gas shows PaO2 6.9 kPa and PaCO2 5.1 kPa. He has never smoked.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Persistent resting hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 7.3 kPa) in advanced pneumoconiosis is an indication for LTOT; NIV is for hypercapnia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Advanced disease with chronic hypoxaemia, no hypercapnia.

elim: For hypercapnic failure; his PaCO2 is normal.
No recurrent infection is described.
Not appropriate at 81 with advanced disease.
Steroids do not help pneumoconiosis.

steps.x: C: Long-term oxygen therapy. Oxygen supportively in advanced disease.

questions.stem: A 70 year old retired coal miner has progressive breathlessness. He worked underground for 35 years and has never smoked. Lung biopsy shows macrophages packed with black dust collected around the respiratory bronchioles, surrounded by collagen and fibroblasts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung disease?
o: Autoimmune attack on the alveolar basement membrane
Inhaled dust triggering chronic inflammation and fibrosis
Protease destruction of alveolar walls without fibrosis
questions.e: Inhaled coal dust is taken up by macrophages, which release mediators that drive chronic inflammation and fibrosis (pneumoconiosis).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung disease?
Dust-laden macrophages and fibrosis.

elim: As in Goodpasture's, not dust disease.
Occupational asthma, not fibrosis.
That is bronchiectasis.
That is emphysema.

steps.x: D: Inhaled dust triggering chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Inhaled particulates trigger chronic inflammation, driving fibrosis in the pneumoconioses.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with silicosis from years of sandblasting develops fever, night sweats and weight loss. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Sputum grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A student asks why silica made him vulnerable.
questions.q: Which cell is primarily damaged by silica in the lung?
questions.e: Silica is directly toxic to alveolar macrophages, causing a fibrogenic cascade and impairing defence against mycobacteria.

steps.x: The question asks: Which cell is primarily damaged by silica in the lung?
Silica kills the cells that would contain TB.

elim: Not the main target of silica.
Not the main target of silica.
Involved in type I allergy, not silica injury.
Produces surfactant; silica mainly kills macrophages.

steps.x: A: Alveolar macrophage. Silica is cytotoxic to alveolar macrophages, triggering fibrosis and predisposing to mycobacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with isocyanate occupational asthma notices that his wheeze starts within 15 minutes of starting to spray paint. He had no asthma before starting the job 3 years ago. Skin testing to an isocyanate-protein conjugate is positive and specific IgE is raised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his immediate reaction?
questions.e: An immediate reaction with specific IgE is IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation; isocyanates can also cause delayed non-IgE, cell-mediated reactions.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his immediate reaction?
Immediate reaction with specific IgE.

elim: Type III, as in hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Mechanism of silica injury.
Mechanism of fibrosis, not acute wheeze.
Causes delayed reactions hours later, not within minutes.

steps.x: D: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation. Isocyanates cause IgE-mediated (immediate) and non-IgE (delayed) sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman works with polyurethane adhesives. Her wheeze and cough start in the evening, 6 to 8 hours after leaving work, and she is woken at night. Specific IgE to isocyanates is negative. A specialist confirms occupational asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her reaction?
o: Direct irritant toxicity with no sensitisation
questions.e: A late asthmatic reaction with negative specific IgE reflects non-IgE, cell-mediated sensitisation to isocyanates; re-exposure causes airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her reaction?

clues: Specific IgE to isocyanates is negative
steps.x: Delayed (late) reaction, IgE negative.

elim: Irritant asthma follows a single heavy exposure, not a delayed pattern every work day.
Causes immediate reactions; her specific IgE is negative.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, with fever and crackles.
Asbestos-related pleural disease.

steps.x: D: Non-IgE, cell-mediated sensitisation. Isocyanates also cause non-IgE-mediated (delayed, cell-mediated) sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 62 year old pigeon breeder has had breathlessness for 4 years. HRCT shows upper and mid zone fibrosis with mosaic attenuation. Lung biopsy shows lymphocytic inflammation around the small airways with loosely formed, non-caseating granulomas and areas of fibrosis.
questions.q: Which best explains how his disease has progressed to fibrosis?
o: Asbestos fibres in the lung interstitium
Chronic bacterial colonisation of dilated bronchi
Chronic type III and type IV hypersensitivity to inhaled antigen
questions.e: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a type III and partly type IV reaction to organic antigen, causing granulomatous inflammation that becomes fibrosis with chronic exposure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains how his disease has progressed to fibrosis?
Organic antigen, granulomatous inflammation, fibrosis.

elim: Asbestosis, with basal fibrosis and pleural plaques.
TB; his granulomas are non-caseating.
Bronchiectasis.
Occupational asthma, which does not cause fibrosis.

steps.x: D: Chronic type III and type IV hypersensitivity to inhaled antigen. HP is a type III (and partly type IV) reaction to inhaled organic antigens; chronic disease progresses to fibrosis.
